strengths: The paper addresses a relevant evaluation problem: shared subjects and shared text stimuli can undermine claims about generalization in brain-to-text decoding. Distinguishing these two sources of overlap is useful.

The empirical investigation covers two modalities, two public datasets, and established decoding models. The BLEU trends across splitting conditions provide suggestive evidence that stimulus overlap can substantially affect reported performance.

Holding out both subjects and stimuli is appropriate for the stated generalization goal. Partitioning fMRI data by stories sensibly addresses overlapping temporal windows. The paper also provides some implementation details and acknowledges that its protocol discards data.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claims exceed the evidence (Section 4.4). Decreasing reconstruction validation loss or improving generation scores with longer training does not itself establish contamination, overfitting, or degraded encoder representations. No text-only, shuffled-signal, or noise-input controls directly establish that the decoder ignores brain signals. A randomly initialized encoder that is subsequently trained is not such a control.

The published splitting algorithms do not enforce their claimed guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership when restoring edges but does not exclude held-out stimuli; Algorithm 2, line 33, checks task membership but does not exclude held-out subjects. Both can therefore reintroduce overlap even from initially disjoint partitions. The loop/index conventions also conflict with the prose description. These may be pseudocode errors, but corrected algorithms and verifiable split assignments are necessary to substantiate the reported zero leakage.

The comparisons do not isolate the magnitude of contamination effects. Splits change the subjects and stories being evaluated, and the proposed method discards an unreported quantity of data. Table 2 also changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together. Matched training budgets, retained-data counts, and controlled overlap comparisons are needed to separate memorization from optimization differences and harder generalization conditions.

The measurement definitions and reported results require correction. Equation (7) intersects individual signal examples although cognitive leakage is defined through shared subjects, and it leaves zero denominators for unseen subjects unspecified. Table 3 reports ROUGE-1 F1 = 84.64 with precision = 63.16 and recall = 71.50 for UniCoRN under method (c), which is incompatible with standard, consistently aggregated F1 scoring. Additionally, Section 4.4.2 describes method (e) as having no text leakage, whereas Table 1 reports 9.29% for fMRI.

The framing overgeneralizes beyond the stated task. Subject overlap is inappropriate for evaluating unseen-subject generalization, but training and testing on different recordings from the same person can be legitimate for personalized decoding. The paper should distinguish evaluation targets rather than characterize all alternative protocols as inherently contaminated.

Reproducibility remains insufficient for a benchmark contribution. Despite claiming a benchmark release, the manuscript provides no code or split-manifest link, exact retained sample counts, discarded-data proportions, or actual seed values. Test-time decoding and checkpoint selection are insufficiently specified. Four seeds are reported for leakage rates, but decoding results lack variability estimates. These concrete soundness and reproducibility gaps prevent a Findings recommendation; targeted corrections and controlled experiments support resubmission next cycle.
